newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD attacks Kohl, won't commit itself to tax talks.
newsitem.headline: SPD attacks Kohl, won't commit itself to tax talks.

text.p: Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Monday continued to attack Chancellor Helmut Kohl's economic policies and gave no sign of returning to the tax reform talks seen needed to ignite the economy and create jobs.

While coalition officials called for the resumption of the stalled talks, SPD leaders said Bonn had lost its grip on the fiscal deficit and stood no chance of meeting the criteria for European monetary union (EMU).

"Of course (Kohl's coalition) know they will not make the deficit criteria with this policy course," Lafontaine told reporters after a meeting of SPD party leaders called to discuss tax reform. Lafontaine again said he was prepared to resume tax talks, but made no mention of a concrete date.

The two sides agree tax cuts are needed to stimulate the economy and boost jobs, but they are wrangling publicly over specific cuts and timing, in what many see as positioning ahead of the 1998 elections.

Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau, of the SPD's inner circle of finance experts, told the news conference the coalition must act to cut non-wage costs such as pensions and social security contributions as soon as possible.

He said tax reform required sound counter-financing, and the administration should stop stressing cuts in the top income tax rate that would benefit only the rich, adding that it should also make no move to cut the solidarity tax as planned in January, 1998.

SPD budget expert Karl Diller said Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans for a net 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in annual tax cuts would create a total financing gap of 160 billion marks in the years 1999 to 2001.
The SPD boycotted tax reform talks slated for March 8 in protest against the government's plans to slash subsidies for coal miners. It has been dancing around the table ever since.
Over the weekend, Waigel urged it to return, and signalled willingness to compromise on a plan to tax income from night- and holiday shifts, one of the key disagreements with the SPD.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats, said the SPD's reluctance to resume talks showed disunity in its ranks.
Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of the Free Democrats (FDP), Kohl's junior coalition partners, said the SPD must decide by Easter if it sees any chance for a consensus.
Meanwhile, Diller said Germany's federal deficit in the first two months of 1997 was two-thirds of the level budgeted for the full year, undermining efforts to qualify for EMU.
The federal deficit totalled 34.8 billion marks in January and February, compared with 53.3 billion marks budgeted for the full year, Diller said, citing Finance Ministry data.
"The causes ... include the fact that expenditures are once again totally out of control," Diller said in a statement.

To qualify for the single European currency, Germany aims to cut its total public sector budget deficit to below 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year from 3.9 percent last year. But many economists are sceptical it will succeed.
The data for 1997 is critical because it forms the basis for deciding which countries participate in EMU from the start.

Waigel aims to cut 1997 government outlays 3.4 percent from last year's level, but in the first two months of the year they were up 2.5 percent, Diller said. Tax revenues, forecast to rise 2.1 percent for the full year, were down 7.1 percent in the two months, he said.
